item.title: Market Outlook: Strong earnings offer support after tech selloff
item.description: Paul Harris examines Canadian earnings and the tech selloff with analysis of Cineplex, Telus, Enbridge and Brookfield Asset Management.
item.dc:creator: BNN Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: Canadian corporate results are in focus as stocks attempt to recover from a sharp technology-led selloff. The latest reports are prompting fresh assessments of business performance and share valuations. BNN Bloomberg spoke with Paul Harris, portfolio manager at Harris Douglas Asset Management, about the earnings season and his views on several Canadian stocks. Key Takeaways Read the full transcript below: LINDSAY: The Nasdaq is attempting that rebound after Thursday’s sharp selloff, led by weakness in chip stocks, and there’s a new batch of Canadian earnings in the mix as well. So let’s bring in Paul Harris, portfolio manager at Harris Douglas Asset Management, to break down some of this. It’s great to have you join us once again. Thank you. PAUL: My pleasure. Thank you for inviting me. LINDSAY: Let’s start with the markets because I wonder what’s driving the market anxiety, I guess, that we’ve been seeing throughout this week and the rebound we’re seeing today. PAUL: Yeah, well, I mean, I was kind of confused by what happened on Wednesday after the kind of Democrats won. I mean, I don’t, I don’t think there — I think there are so many of the issues that the markets face still out there. Whether it’s Iran, whether it’s maybe Ukraine, whether it’s higher oil prices, whether it’s interest rates going up — or, you know, they’ve come down lately because of what’s happening in the stock market. But I think those issues are still out there, and I think that they’re, they are very, you know — and all this issue with AI being, the AI trade being such a big part of what’s happened with the stock market. So I think these are very big issues, and I think that it’s hard to kind of understand what’s going to happen with a new Congress starting in January. And so the market’s kind of running up like that and coming back, coming down yesterday, I think kind of evens out stuff. And I think the market really has to find a footing about how they deal, how we are going to deal with many of these issues going forward. LINDSAY: Yeah, and I wonder where it goes from here, right? Like, do you think investors should brace for more downside before markets maybe eventually find a floor? PAUL: Well, I think certainly there, you know, I think there’s certainly more potential for that, or more volatility, I would say, right? But I think that going into the end of November, and — but usually you get a rally in December from a seasonal point of view. So I think that there’s a, there’s a chance that you may see more volatility. I think you saw the VIX sort of run up so high yesterday, which is almost like a point where, you know, it gets to where you think about buying the market, right? So I think that there’s a — you can expect more volatility. I think the, you know, there are many things, like if you look at earnings, they were quite good over the, over the quarter, right? So I think there is some, there’s some foundation there that helps the stock market. I think the issue becomes how we think about, you know, what happens with AI data centres, all these things. You know, I don’t think they stop, but I think there may be a, you know, a cooling down of how quickly they’re going to get to be able to build these things out, right? So, so I think there’s, there are, there are many kind of issues that the market faces, but I think that the underlying issue of, you know, good earnings has shown up again in this quarter. I think that, I think that you’ll continue to see that going forward, and I think the rates are lower, right? So it helps a little bit. LINDSAY: You talked about earnings, so I want to get to that because we’re not done with earnings season yet. We have a whole slew coming out today, of course, as you know. I want to ask you about some of them. Cineplex is what we’ll start with. It reported record quarterly revenue. I wonder what you make of that. Like, is this a turnaround story that’s gaining momentum? PAUL: You know, it’s hard. I mean, I don’t like Cineplex at all because I think it’s a — like, if you look at the numbers, yes, they were very good, but they came because there were two big, really big hits, right? So they’re kind of stuck in the situation where, if you have these really big, big blockbusters, then they do very well, especially on the premium side. You can see that concessions were down a little bit, but I think that, you know, I think that the issue of streaming will continue to dominate this kind of, that industry. And I think that they’re going to continue to have trouble, you know, over the long term, that people are just more and more willing to watch a movie at home, and it’s much easier and more enjoyable in some ways, right? I think these big blockbusters make a difference. You can’t — I mean, The Odyssey would have been much better to see in a cinema than probably in your home theatre, but I think that’s not, that’s not — those are just a few films each year, right? So they’re very dependent on these blockbusters, and if you don’t have one in a year, I think it’s much more difficult. LINDSAY: Yeah, a very good point. OK, Telus, in the meantime, missed expectations. What went wrong in this quarter for Telus? PAUL: Well, you know, I think it’s funny when we listen to analysts talk about Telus because, to me, Telus is a, is a real story that’s going to change over a period of time. It’s a company we own. You know, they have a new CEO. He’s sort of going through and thinking about how to make the company better, whether from a financial footing, which is one of the things because they’re looking at cost cuts, but also, you know, trying to drive new revenue, maybe even get rid of some of the assets that they don’t really want to keep on their books — Telus non-core assets, non-telecom assets. So I think you have to give them a chance to kind of review the whole company and then, from there, kind of make a decision about, you know, what Telus is going to look like over the next several years. I think it’s probably a stock you want to buy, even though it’s, you know, it’s at these levels, because I think that, you know, they’ve cut their dividend. They’re going to move on from that. I think they’re going to have better financial stability if they can get all those cost cuts in, and they can really kind of review their businesses and pick the best businesses that are growing the best for them. LINDSAY: Enbridge also reported a rise in profit, and they’re attributing that to strength in the natural gas business. What’s your thesis on this stock? Do you like … PAUL: Well, so we own Enbridge. We’ve owned it for a long time. We really like it. I mean, I think the natural gas side did well. I think the power infrastructure is doing well. You know, I think that Enbridge is kind of in a little bit of a, in my view, a bit of a sweet spot with what’s going on with their ability to help on the data centre side. You know, natural gas is a, is a very, is a much cheaper and better product to use than other areas of, in — if you’re looking at energy. And I think the pipeline guys have done really well. So, you know, being able to supply all these things. So it’s Enbridge. I think at these levels, you can, you should be buying here. LINDSAY: OK, and then lastly, I wanted to ask you also about Brookfield Asset Management. Brookfield Asset Management met expectations, but — so I wonder, like, do you see the current environment creating more opportunities for the firm or, or really just more challenges going forward? PAUL: Well, I think, like, this is the, this is the core — like, this is a great environment for Brookfield, right? I mean, first of all, when you look at their numbers, they raised $25 million in the quarter, $123 billion for the year, right? So their kind of fees were up. All those things were up. In my view, they were good numbers. I think what you have to remember is where they really perform well is environments of volatility because they can buy up cheaper assets, right? So for them, I think for them, it’s always this environment when they have volatility. When certain areas are not doing well relative to other areas, they can, they can come in and provide the capital that is needed for businesses either to borrow from or to buy assets that they want, whether it’s property, whether it’s infrastructure. So they have that ability, and they’ve been very good at this over long periods of time, right? So it’s a very unique company in this country that has been able to, you know, look at purely very much like a value investor, right? They kind of wait around. They have all this money, and they’ll deploy it when it’s the right time. I think that’s what you’re paying them for. That’s what you’re paying those fees for because they’re able to do that very successfully over long periods of time. So I, you know, we don’t own Brookfield Asset Management. We own Brookfield Corp. But I think Brookfield Asset Management is equally a great asset to own. LINDSAY: OK, we’ll leave it there. Paul Harris, portfolio manager at Harris Douglas Asset Management. Always great to have you join us. Thank you. --- This BNN Bloomberg summary and transcript of the Nov. 6, 2026 interview with Paul Harris are published with the assistance of AI. item.title: Unemployment rate rose to 6.7% in October, StatCan says
item.description: Canada’s unemployment rate went up to a six-month high in October and the economy lost a few thousand jobs as the private sector and full-time employment saw declines, data showed on Friday.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — Some economists are getting worried that a string of job losses in recent months is revealing cracks in the labour market. Statistics Canada said Friday that the unemployment rate rose two tenths of a point to 6.7 per cent in October. The labour market shed 4,700 jobs last month, the agency said, and more people were also looking for work. October’s modest decline followed a cumulative loss of 110,000 jobs across September and August. A Reuters poll of economists had expected the economy would bounce back with a gain of 13,600 jobs in October. “For anyone hoping that October would bring a recovery in the Canadian job market after back-to-back negative surprises, today’s release is a disappointment,” said Sneha Puri, economist with jobs search site Indeed, in a media statement. Private sector employment fell by 53,000 positions last month, marking the first decline in the segment since February. Employment in the public sector, meanwhile, was up 50,000 positions. StatCan noted that, on a year-over-year basis, private sector jobs are still up while the public sector is down. Employment in the wholesale and retail trade industry has trended down over the past year and the sector led losses in October, shedding 29,000 roles. Transportation and warehousing and food and accommodation also posted losses last month, offset by some gains in construction and education. CIBC senior economist Andrew Grantham said in an interview that he had expected more of a lift in the October labour market from one-time factors like the Alberta referendum. While he had been anticipating the jobless rate would tick up in the fourth quarter in the face of tariff-related headwinds, Friday’s employment figures suggest there’s more underlying softness in the jobs market. “It does look as if we’re seeing some weakness in the labour market outside of those trade-sensitive areas. So that’s a concern for us right now,” Grantham said. That could dampen expectations for a rebound in job growth in 2027, he added. The unemployment rate for young workers aged 15 to 24 jumped to 13.7 per cent in October, up 0.7 percentage points from September, as employment edged down and more youth looked for work. Young workers have faced a generally tough labour market in recent years but there had been little change in the jobless rate for the age group over the summer. StatCan said the unemployment rate was higher for students compared with youth not attending school. The agency said the layoff rate – the proportion of people employed in September who were laid off by October – was “virtually unchanged” compared with a year earlier at 0.7 per cent. Average hourly wages rose 2.2 per cent annually in October, edging down from 2.3 per cent in September. Puri said Indeed’s Canadian job postings ticked up at the end of last month, which could be an indication of future hiring. If Canada can gain clarity on U.S. trade policy in the wake of the midterm elections this week, she said that could give employers the confidence to hire again. “If this optimism isn’t then translated into a strong jobs report in the months ahead, the surprising weakness in headline employment will start to look less temporary and more like the beginning of a renewed cooling in the labour market,” Puri warned. The October job figures come a little over a week after the Bank of Canada delivered its first interest rate hike in more than three years, raising its policy rate by a quarter point to 2.5 per cent. Thomas Ryan, senior North America economist at Capital Economics, said in a note to clients that the uptick in the unemployment rate and muted wage growth should tell the Bank of Canada that there’s still slack in the job market right now. The October jobs data should therefore push back on calls for much more tightening of monetary policy, he argued. “Ultimately, this adds to our conviction that the bank will hike rates no more than twice more as a precaution against upside inflation risks, before calling it a day,” Ryan said. Financial market odds of another quarter-point hike at the Bank of Canada’s final rate decision of the year on Dec. 9 stood at 35 per cent as of Friday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. Bank of Canada officials made clear after the October rate hike that their focus is on getting ahead of inflationary pressures spreading from the global energy shock, Grantham noted. Soft labour market data and recent declines in the benchmark price of oil take pressure of the central bank to deliver another rate hike next month, he said. “We have a lot of days for oil prices to do something volatile between now and December. But if those two forces stay in effect, we do forecast that they will hold interest rates at the December meeting,” Grantham said. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026. By Craig Lord
